newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Scientists discuss British plan to ease beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Scientists discuss British plan to ease beef ban.

text.p: The European Union's Scientific Veterinary Committee met on Wednesday amid doubts that they would approve a British proposal to ease a worldwide ban on its beef exports by exempting herds certified to be free of mad cow disease.

Britain proposed in February that the ban, which was imposed in March 1996, should be partially lifted to allow exports of beef from Northern Irish and other herds guaranteed to be free of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
"It's doubtful that the scientists will recommend approval of the certified herd scheme. They are more likely to raise questions and call for further explanation," said an EU source.
The ban was imposed after Britain said that BSE could be transmitted to humans who ate infected beef.
EU sources said that although advice from a sub-group of veterinary experts was confused it still raised doubts about the efficiency of computerised systems for tracking animal movements.
The sub-group also called for clarification about how the scheme would work.

In a joint letter in April, EU Food Safety and Farm Commissioners Emma Bonino and Franz Fischler cast doubts about how the complex scheme would work, especially in Scotland and England where computerised records are very recent.

Even in Northern Ireland, where a computerised system was set up in 1988 to record cattle movements from birth to slaughter as well as BSE and other animal illnesses, there were doubts about whether all suspect animals were identified.

The meeting of the independent scientists was expected to continue into the afternoon. The Commission will then consider their advice after which it could present a proposal to the Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials.
